paragraphs: Friend, here's what I see in this whole chapter: God takes blood, people and justice seriously, even when nobody is looking. When a killing can't be solved, the elders still come out, still measure, still own it before the LORD, and they don't shrug and go home. Then Moses says the bloodshed will be atoned for, so the guilt gets dealt with (Deuteronomy 21:8-9).

Now look at who gets protected in the rest of it. The captive woman gets time to mourn her father and mother, and if the man isn't pleased with her, he can't sell her or treat her as a slave, "since you have dishonored her" (Deuteronomy 21:14). The unloved wife's son keeps the firstborn's place, because "the right of the firstborn belongs to him" (Deuteronomy 21:17). Feelings don't get to rewrite what is owed to a person, though I think the rebellious son's case is heavy, and Moses says it is to purge the evil so all Israel hears and is afraid (Deuteronomy 21:21).

Then comes the tree. Anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse, so the body gets buried that day (Deuteronomy 21:23). Friend, hold onto that line, because Paul, an apostle of Jesus, points back to it and writes that Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). That's why this old rule matters to you today: Jesus took on that curse for us, and that is love worth remembering.
